text:
Thanks. I thought the survey was pretty clear overall, though Q3 felt a bit relentless – each addition felt like another step too far. It’s hard to weigh small improvements against privacy concerns without knowing *how* that data will be used and secured in practice.

I think questions around explainability (Q4) are key; we need advisors to understand why a student is flagged, so they can actually help. 

My answers diverged a little on sensitive data – I was stricter than most, saying “never” for age, gender, race… because of my own experience restarting after dropping out. It felt like adding those things could reinforce biases or punish students for circumstances beyond their control. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism would help address that anxiety?

Thanks. I agree with S1 – Q3 did feel like a slippery slope. Each addition seemed to push further into potentially sensitive areas, and it was hard to assess the benefit without knowing *exactly* what 'improvement' meant in practice.

I think Q5, about fairness, is absolutely vital. As an international student still adjusting, I’m acutely aware of how systems can unintentionally disadvantage certain groups. Losing a bit of overall accuracy to ensure fairer outcomes feels like the right trade-off – and equal recall seems crucial here. 

My responses were perhaps more open to using nationality or first-gen status *if* it improved identification, because those experiences might genuinely contribute to academic challenges for newcomers like me. But always with strong safeguards.

Thanks both of you. I also found Q3 quite difficult – it *did* feel relentless, and that’s a good way to put it. It's hard to say 'yes' to adding data without knowing the specifics of how it will be protected. And “improvement” felt very abstract; what does that actually look like for a student?

I completely agree with S1 about explainability being key, and I think my stricter stance on sensitive data stems from similar anxieties – rebuilding after dropping out means feeling particularly vulnerable to judgement. 

I was surprised more people weren't as hesitant on things like nationality. Perhaps an opt-out *would* address some concerns, allowing students to control their own data even if the model technically benefits from it. That feels like a good compromise, especially given my experience navigating a new system and language.

Thanks. I agree with S1, S5 & S6 – Q3 *was* relentless, and that feeling of adding data without knowing exactly how it’s used is unsettling. As someone with ADHD who restarted my studies, I'm hyperaware of being categorised. “Improvement” felt too vague; does a 1% increase justify adding something deeply personal?

Explainability (Q4) is vital for trust – and that’s huge for me, given past experiences. I was stricter on nearly all sensitive data because it feels like piling onto already vulnerable students. Seeing so many 'never' answers on age/gender/race gives me some relief! 

I’m glad the group prioritised equal recall (Q5). And an opt-out? Absolutely essential. Students *need* control over their data, even if it means slightly less “accuracy”.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *did* feel like a constant push for more data, and it was hard to gauge the real benefit versus risk. Especially coming from the Faroe Islands and restarting my studies here, I'm acutely aware of being seen as 'different'. 

I think questions around fairness (Q5) and explainability (Q4) are paramount. It’s easy for systems to unintentionally disadvantage students like me, so equal recall is crucial. I was stricter on sensitive data – age, gender, nationality - because labels can be really damaging after a dropout experience. Seeing others share that makes me hopeful. 

I strongly support the opt-out idea; giving students control feels vital for trust and agency.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – particularly about Q3 feeling relentless and the need to know *exactly* how data will be used and secured. As an international student working part-time, I'm especially cautious about sharing personal information. "Improvement" needs clear definition; it's easy to lose sight of individual wellbeing chasing a small percentage point. 

I think Q4 – explainability – is crucial for building trust with advisors. My answers reflected that caution around sensitive data. Nationality and first-gen status *could* be relevant, but potentially reinforce existing biases against international students. The opt-out mechanism feels vital; giving us control over our data would address my biggest concern. I also strongly agree with prioritising equal recall – fairness has to come first.

Thanks everyone. I wholeheartedly agree with the points raised about Q3 feeling relentless and the need for concrete details on data security – it’s essential we're clear on *how* this information is protected before adding anything. As an advisor, I see students’ vulnerabilities firsthand, so my hesitations around sensitive data are strong.

I think Q4, explainability, is paramount; as advisors, we need to understand the ‘why’ behind a flag to offer appropriate support – it’s not just about identifying risk, but understanding its roots. My answers reflected that caution. The emphasis on equal recall in Q5 also resonates deeply; fairness must be central to this system. And I fully endorse the opt-out idea - empowering students with control is vital for building trust and ensuring ethical implementation.

Thanks everyone. I agree completely with the points made about Q3 – it *did* feel like a cascade of data requests, and ‘improvement’ felt very abstract without knowing the practical impact. As an advisor for six years, I see firsthand how quickly things can go wrong for students, so protecting their privacy feels paramount.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely vital; we need to understand *why* a student is flagged to offer truly effective support. My answers were cautious on sensitive data – even with safeguards, there’s a risk of reinforcing existing inequalities. The opt-out suggestion is excellent - student agency is key. I also strongly support prioritising equal recall (Q5); fairness isn't negotiable. It felt good to see so much alignment around those principles.

Thanks everyone. I echo a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *did* feel like an escalating request for data, and that abstract “improvement” metric was hard to grapple with without knowing its real-world impact on students. As someone who's been advising for eleven years, I see how easily students can fall through the cracks, so identifying risk early is important, but not at any cost.

I strongly agree explainability (Q4) is paramount – we need to understand *why* a student’s flagged to offer meaningful support, and build trust. I was stricter on sensitive data; it feels ethically problematic without incredibly robust safeguards. The opt-out mechanism is vital, empowering students to control their information. And yes, fairness—equal recall—has to be central.

Thanks everyone. I definitely agree with the feeling that Q3 was… a lot. As someone restarting after a break due to my mental health, it felt like each added data point risked oversimplifying really complex situations and potentially misinterpreting things. The “improvement” metric felt too abstract – what *actually* changes for a student?

I think explainability (Q4) is crucial. If an advisor can’t understand *why* I was flagged, how can they offer helpful support? My answers were stricter on sensitive data because of my own vulnerability and past experiences. Seeing so much alignment around that makes me feel relieved. And the opt-out mechanism… absolutely essential. We need control over our data, especially when dealing with something as personal as academic struggles.

Thanks everyone. I agree wholeheartedly about Q3 feeling relentless – each addition felt like a step too far into my private life. As someone managing a chronic health condition while finishing my thesis, and having used disability services, data privacy is *hugely* important to me. ‘Improvement’ needs real-world context; it’s easy to get lost in percentages.

I think explainability (Q4) is vital for building trust with advisors. My answers were stricter on sensitive data – nationality, race - because past experiences make me wary of categorisation. Seeing the group prioritise fairness and an opt-out mechanism is really reassuring. Giving students control over their data feels like a fundamental right, especially when dealing with health vulnerabilities.

Thanks everyone. I completely agree that Q3 felt… overwhelming. As someone with dyslexia who’s just started university again, it feels like constantly being assessed and categorised. That “improvement” metric really bothered me – what does a small percentage point actually *mean* for a student's wellbeing? 

For me, explainability is huge - I need to understand why anything is happening, given my learning differences. My stricter answers on sensitive data come from feeling vulnerable; I don’t want labels reinforcing negative perceptions. It was good to see so many people feel that way. And the opt-out mechanism is essential – control over my own data feels vital, especially when it comes to something as personal as academic struggles.
